item.title: Importing Course Content into Moodle (XML to HTML)
item.dc:creator: hasslethishoff
item.content:encoded:
XML to Moodle – Running QuickScript

QuickScript is a scripting tool that is used to convert XML files to HTML.

  • Open O:\Open Learning Share\IDRG-production\SOFTWARE\XML_SCRIPTING
  • Double-click: -=QuickScript.jar (shortcut can be saved to desktop)
  • XML files should be named with the course code plus the relevant master number. For example, mngt4781_sw5.xml.
  • Once scripted, HTML files will be placed in O:\Open Learning Share\IDRG-production\SOFTWARE\XML_SCRIPTING\COURSES_OUTPUT.
  • Copy and paste Images and Resources folders into scripted folder, highlight all files, and zip
  • Run Moodle Backup Producer (username: moodle, password: producer) using zipped file to create file for Moodle upload. Settings shown below.
  • Download file and upload content to Moodle (Refer to Moodle Settings: Backup/Restore/Merge)

item.title: Moodle Settings: Backup/Restore/Merge
item.dc:creator: hasslethishoff
item.content:encoded:
Container Backup

  1. Click More, and then Course reuse. On the next page, use the dropdown to select Backup.
  1. Select the following items and click the Next button
    • Include activities and resources
    • Include blocks
    • Include files
    • Include filters
    • Include question bank
    • Include groups and groupings
  1. If we are going to be restoring the backup to a LIVE container, deselect the DO NOT COPY tab in the Schema settings and click the Next button
  1. On the Confirmation and review page, scan the settings/options to ensure everything looks correct and if there are no issues, click the Perform backup button.
  1. Once the backup process is complete, you should see a "The backup file was successfully created." message, and you can click Continue.

Container Restore

  1. Click More, and then Course reuse. On the next page, use the dropdown to select Restore.
  1. If you're using the Moodle Packager or have previously downloaded a Moodle backup, you can upload the file to the Import a backup file and click the Restore button or locate the backup file in the User private backup area and click the Restore link.
  1. Review the Moodle backup details on the Confirm screen and click the Next button.
  1. Locate the Restore into this course section, select Delete the contents of this course and then restore and click the Continue button.

IMPORTANT: Double-check you are in the correct container, as this option will completely erase the current content.

  1. On the Settings page, the following items should be selected and click the Next button.
    • Include activities and resources
    • Include blocks
    • Include filters
    • Include groups and groupings
  1. On the Schema page, we usually don't need to adjust any of the settings, but you can adjust the container names and deselect items that are not required and click the Next button.
  1. In the next section, review the Restore settings and confirm the details. If everything looks correct, click the Preform restore button at the bottom of the page.
  1. Once the Restore process is complete, you should see a "The Backup file was successfully restored." message, and you can click Continue.

Merge Container Content

Moodle content can be added from a backup file or other container using the Merge option during the restore process. Merging content follows the same steps as a full restore, with two adjustments in the process:

  • On the Destination page, under Restore into this course, select "Merge the backup into this course"
  • On the Schema page, only select the sections/tabs and content/activities/items you want to import

After those adjustments are made, you can complete the Restore process and the selected items should be added to the Moodle container.

IMPORTANT: The Merge process will not replace anything currently in a Moodle container, it only pulls in the new items so if there is already content in the section (e.g. the Course Guide toggles, Books, etc.), you'll have duplicate items (original content and new content).

item.title: Word to XML - Setting up Word Documents for QuickTagIt (XML)
item.dc:creator: bforsyth
item.content:encoded:
Course content documents are received in Word format, which need to be converted to XML using QuickTagIt, an XML scripting tool that is used to convert .docx files into .xml files. Quicktagit uses specific word document structures to identify how to create the XML document. Make sure you have added the OL Styles Template and follow the steps below.

Important: You can start to format your document, save, and quickly script to XML to see if you’re getting the required XML structure for the OL course. Scripting at this stage take minimal time and will help spot initial problems before moving to the next step.

Step 1: General Cleanup

Remove any extra content (title page, table of contents, page breaks, etc.).

Step 2: Adjust Heading Levels

How Heading Levels Convert in XML

Courses with Books (currently the most common structure used):

  • Heading 1: creates an objectgroup in XML = Book in Moodle
  • Heading 2: creates a nested objectgroup in XML = Book Page in Moodle
  • Heading 3: creates a topic in XML = topics within a Book Page
  • Heading 4 and greater (to maximum of 5): Shows at text within above topic in XML = display as normal content text within the above page in Moodle
  • Heading 5 should be used for all notebox headings.

Basic Course with Tabs (no longer commonly used):

  • Heading 1: creates an objectgroup in XML = a folder in HTML = Tab
  • Heading 2: creates a topic in XML = a HTML page within folder = Label within Tab
  • Heading 3 and greater (to maximum of 5): act as normal headings within HTML pages = display as normal content text within Label

Steps for Adjusting Heading Levels

The easiest method to adjust heading levels is using Outline view. If headings are not included in the document then manually add using Styles.

Following is an example of the heading levels of a standard Course Guide:

Reminder: Heading 1 (Course Guide) will display as a book, while Heading 2 will display as a chapter within the book.

Following is an example of the heading levels of a standard Course Guide:

Reminder: Heading 1 (Module 1) will display as a book, while Heading 2 (Introduction, Module 1 Overview, Topic 1 etc.) will display as a chapter within the book.

Additional Heading Formatting Considerations

In addition to adjusting heading levels, it may be necessary to move entire sections or add additional headings to better fit Moodle’s book layout and improve navigation. For example:

  • When linking assignment or quiz activity, add title using normal bold text (will enable autolinking once in Moodle).
  • IF assignment/discussion forum instructions are duplicated within modules, provide brief information (e.g. Assignment X is worth XX% of your final grade. For more information on Assignment X, view the Assessments Overview tab).
  • IF assignment/discussion forum have not been provided in separate documents, extract assessment information into separate files (create Assessments Overview and Discussions tabs using H1).

Step 3: Extracting Images and Equations

Images

Refer to the Copyright Report while working through this step to ensure that image captions/attributions are accurate.

Two Ways to Extract Images:

  1. Change the file's extension to .zip, then copy images from the media folder within
  2. Right click on individual images and select "Save As"
    • Image files should be named in the following format:
      course code_location in course_figure number/caption/general description.

Image size:

  • Minimum: Big enough to see clearly
  • Maximum: 750px by 600px.

Tip: If an image looks distorted upon loading course content into Moodle, you can click on the Image in the Moodle editor, select “Insert/Edit Image,” then check “autosize” so it will resize the image to be proportional.

Equations

Equations in Word documents can be either Word equation editor or MathType equation editor. We want all equations to be MathType equations. MathType should show up as a separate tab in your Word install.

Creating/Editing an Equation in Word

For Creation: Click on the MathType tab, and then on the far left ‘Inline’. This will bring up the MathType equation editor.

For Editing: Double Click on equation to open up editor

Mathtype Editor

In Mathtype, you build up equations by selecting formatting and adding to boxes. Start with the larger structures and work to finer. For example: choosing a horizontal fraction first then filling in upper and lower terms.

Inside this editor there are a few main keyboard shortcuts to save time:

When you are done your equation, close and save the equation (will show up in Word). We will now convert it to LaTeX.

Converting MathType to LaTeX

MathType can convert to a Moodle friendly format using the conversion tool MathJax:LaTex. This code will make it through the XML to HTML process. Converting removes original formatting, so save a copy of the original document before converting.

To convert to MathType, select the MathType tab, “Convert Equations,” and ensure “Text using MathType Translator:” is set to MathJax:LaTeX. You may select to convert the whole document or only the currently selected text.

OR

Use the bulk export function in MathType to extract equations as images. The resolution of images created can be controlled by setting within MathType.

Note: Equations need to be in Mathtype format for extraction to work.

Formatting LaTeX

Once Word converts equations to LaTeX, there are several changes that need to be made.

The 'rm' Tag

This tag is what is generated for raw text inputs (when you want to use letters or ensure there are spaces at certain spots in the equation). It is handy to select the latex code and click “Replace,” and then replace all ‘rm’ instances with ‘text’. Be sure to check “Find whole words only.” This will ensure the code works in WordPress with MathJax.

Beginning and End

Word adds “\(“ at the beginning and “\)” at the end of its LaTeX creations.

  • Moodle/ XML
    In Moodle/XML "\( latex code \)" will place the equation inline with the text and "$$ latex code $$" will display the equation on a new line the center of the page. Note that everything within the backslash brackets or everything within a double dollar sign becomes a full equation no matter how many lines it has.
    Examples:
    Inline - Using the following formula \({\text{I = Prt}}\) to calculate the interest.
    Centered - $$ml = \frac{{15}}{{100ml}} \times 500ml = 75ml$$

Tip: You can use http://bandicoot.maths.adelaide.edu.au/MathJax/test/sample-dynamic-2.html or https://quicklatex.com/ to test out the examples above and your equation formatting.

  • WordPress
    In WordPress these need to be removed and at the beginning of the equation ‘$latex=’ needs to be added and at the end ‘$’ needs to be added. If these changes are not made, the equations won’t work in WordPress.

Multiline equations

If there is need for multiline equations, it is often necessary that the equals sign is the lineup point for each line. This can be achieved by using several tools:

  • \begin{array}{rcl}
    • This line goes at the start of the code, right after $latex=
    • It starts an array, and defines the number of columns and their alignment with {rcl}
    • {rcl} means the first column will be right justified, the second column centered, and the third column left justified
  • &
    • This symbol denotes a new column, and in a three column system should be on either side of the equals sign
  • \\
    • This symbol denotes a new line, and should go at the end of an equation, right before the next equation starts
  • \end{array}
    • This line goes at the end of the code, right before the closing $

Other Syntax (for editing directly in LaTeX code)

Fractions

Fractions can be inserted using the following syntax:
\frac{{...}}{{...}}
Where the first set of curly brackets is the upper part of the fraction and the second pair is the lower part of the fraction.

Text

Text can be inserted using the following syntax:
{\text{…}}
Where the desired text would be inserted inside the curly brackets in place of the dots. The text will appear exactly as entered, preserving any included whitespace.

Superscript

Used for exponents, requires the following syntax:
^{…}
Where the desired exponent/superscript element would be inserted inside the curly brackets in place of the dots.

Subscript

Subscript can be achieved using the following syntax:
_{…}
Where the desired subscript element would be inserted inside the curly brackets in place of the dots.

Nesting

Note that all of these can be nested. For example:
35^{(\frac{{25}}{{365}})}
Will produce:

Step 4: Updating Copyright Information and Linking Files

The Copyright team will generate a Copyright Report for each course that we work on, and in most cases we will have that document when we start work on a course. If not, we'll request it when we start the development process. It is recommended to complete the required copyright adjustment while formatting Word documents to avoid additional work further along the production process, such as in XML or Moodle.

Using the Copyright instructions, we'll want to make the following updates to our Word documents before scripting.

  • Update/add/replace image captions, attributions, etc.
  • Add video captions/attributions (easy to copy/drag in XML)
  • Download and link files (CTRL+K) including PDF, Word, PowerPoint, etc. as this will automatically generate the graphic entities and objectref tags needed in XML

Unfortunately, it's not possible to embed media objects such as videos and H5P objects from Word.

item.title: Additional Formatting/Copyright Considerations
item.dc:creator: hasslethishoff
item.content:encoded:
Recent updates:
- Added details around Course Guide Assessments table and removing the "Mandatory" wording
- Added Workflow/Information Updates From Copyright section on communications from Editing/Copyright Supervisor.
- Added Autolinking Moodle Resources (Files) and Activities section describing autolinking and updated information regarding autolink formatting.

Workflow/Information Updates From Copyright

The Copyright/Editing Supervisor, Chris Ward, has provided the following information to help address some of the Copyright challenges we've been experiences. I have summarized some of the details and added Production specific information in italics. If there are any question, please reach out to the Production Supervisor.

  • Copyright D4P Updates: Copyright specialists will share updates in D4P so the site will be more useful as a resource. This won’t help with errors, but it should help with general (“where’s the report”) work flow questions. Production will still include Copyright in the "Start Work" communication, but check D4P for Copyright updates if we haven't received the file in a timely manner instead of sending out multiple requests for the report document.
  • CC Chris Ward, (cward@tru.ca) on queries or follow-ups: There is only one copyright specialist for every maintenance course, and they also work on face-to-face course packs and expired records. If Production is not receiving the information needed after an email or two, we should loop Chris in on the communications.
  • Copyright Communication with Editors: Editors have more time than copyright specialists to look at courses and consider consistency, accuracy, style or faculty requests. Editors and IDs should report 3rd-party content in courses, but we’ve never had a standardized practice. This week a copyright specialist is meeting with editors to discuss communication from editors to IPO. It is IPO’s job to track 3rd-part content in courses; however, consistent communication from editors should help to prevent missed items. From a Production perspective, hopefully this additional communication between IPO and Editors will help reduce the number of items missed in the reports received.
  • Copyright Communication with ESTs: Excel is the output from FileMaker, but Copyright has better options like email or meetings via Teams to continue the collaboration or refine the shared information. This one is a bit tricky for Production as the Copyright document is our main source of information, so in most cases we're directly referencing the document for our questions. If there are situations where an online meeting would be helpful, feel free to arrage that with a Copyright specialist.
  • IPO doesn’t track links. As a general policy links are not included on a copyright report. In certain instances some copyright specialists do include links in a copyright spreadsheet for major or new courses. They do this because it might be uncertain whether the item will be a linked or hosted (Post to LMS) when they first identify it in the Word document. By making an entry on the spreadsheet, they can verify later if they’ve identified and tracked all the 3rd-party content in a course. Because of this, some links do make it into FileMaker and into the copyright report. Their practice is to not track links, but you will find them in some new or major revision courses. Copyright's focus is on the hosted (post to LMS) entries. Production is mainly concerned with Post in LMS items as well, with the exception of YouTube videos as they are often embedded and we require the correct attribution information from Copyrightt
  • FileMaker and terminology: Copyright is continuing to train and focus on this. (FileMaker is not an easy interface to learn.) They have talked about simplifying or clarifying the fields, but that is probably a long-term goal rather than something that can implement now. The fields are based on the paperwork required by Access Copyright many years ago which is no longer uses. With so many details to capture, errors in one field don’t exactly stand out. No direct impact on Production at the moment, but hopefully future discussion may help align the information to reduce the number of issues we see.

Reviewing the Copyright Report & Extracting Reading Files

Refer to the Copyright Report as you work through Word documents to ensure that sources are cited correctly and to save any files that have been cleared to be hosted in Moodle (if we have not been provided with them).

When we are sent a copyright report, it will say Link, or Post in LMS for all materials. Copyright uses different language than Production so refer to the following for clarification:

  • Images
    • Material type: will say IMAGE or DIAGRAM
    • Material reproduction type: For images, Post in LMS, means the image should be directly inserted into Moodle.
    • Material Caption and Material Credit Line Text: Make sure you add the caption if included, and the reference should either be in the reference list at the end of the Module, or add an attribution with the Material Credit Line Text.
  • Videos
    • Material type: will say VIDEO
    • Material reproduction type: For videos, Post in LMS, means the video is, or should be, hosted on Barabus (which Jon does) and should be directly in Moodle. Link mean the video should be embedded if possible, but not hosted on Barabus.
    • Material Caption and Material Credit Line Text: There is often no caption. Material Credit Line text should be added as an attribution, especially if you are embedding a video that we are not hosting.

Files should be saved in the following format: course code_ general location_ author and/or title. For example, “MNGT4781_M2_Lowenstein.”

The Copyright Report may also provide replacement links for readings that are to remain as links, including links to access material through the TRU library to ensure that the full text is available. Ensure that links are provided through the title of the resource rather than a URL.

Hosting Articles/Blogs from the Web

Readings from websites can be optimized for PDF using tools such as https://www.printfriendly.com/.

Title Pages for Readings

All externally created resources hosted in Moodle must include a title page. These may include articles, readings, or any resource in which we receive permission to host in PDF form. Generally, title pages are not included for internally-created documents (which do not require a copyright line).

Using OL Production Tools Application and Excel Template

Use the Excel template located in the Production Tools folder (O:\Open Learning Share\IDRG-production\SOFTWARE\PRODUCTION TOOLS) and the OL Production Tools application to create multiple copyright title pages for items in the copyright report.

  1. Create a copy of the Resource Title Page Generator Template.xlsx document on your desktop
  2. Copy/paste the copyright credit information into the Material Credit Line Text column
  3. Copy/paste resource title into the Material Excerpt Title column
  4. Save file and close Excel document
  5. Open the OL Production Tools application (O:\Open Learning Share\IDRG-production\SOFTWARE\PRODUCTION TOOLS) and select the © Title Pages tab
  6. Select the template as the source file, enter the course code and course title, select Output Location and click the Generate button

Problems Adding the Title Page

Occasionally an original file may be locked and prevent you from adding the title page. In this case:

  • Check with the course lead. Possible solutions:
    • Adding the credit line directly into the page XML if the resource is listed there.
    • Adding the credit line under the posted resource link by adding it to the file description in Moodle and selecting “Display description on course page”. Use subscript to reduce size.
  • Ensure that the solution is acceptable to the license given (i.e. simply posting a resource without a title page or credit line anywhere would not work with a license that mandates a credit line be shown).

Resizing PDF Resource Pages

It is common that extracted or provided readings need to be resized. To do so, simply select File -> Print -> Adobe PDF and the document will resize to a standard 8.5 x 11”.

Preparing Scanned PDF Files

Often texbook and other resource scans will include two side-by-side pages that need to be adjusted into a single page layout for optimal viewing and printing for students. Use the information below to crop, combine and create course-ready PDF from scanned materails:

  • Make a copy of your scanned PDF document and add "_odd" to the file name as we'll use the file to crop the odd pages.
  • Open the "_odd" document > Go to Edit and select the Crop tool
  • On the odd page, use your mouse to draw a box around the page content you want to capture
    • It's possible to crop all the odd pages as once if the scanned content is uniform enough to fit with the cropping area. Adjust your box size accordingly to capture content across all odd pages in document if possible.
    • If variations of the scanned content can't be cropped at once you can crop pages individually.
  • Once you cropping area is selected, double-click to open the Croping options
    • If cropping all ddd pages, in the Page Ranges section select All
    • If cropping single odd page, in the Page Ranges confirm correct page is in the From section
  • After cropping, scroll through the pages to confirm no content was cut off and adjust if needed (You can use Undo)
  • Once you have cropped all the odd pages, save your document and close
  • Use the same steps above to crop the Even pages from the original document and save
  • Open your Even and Odd documents side by side, open the Pages navigation panel and drag/drop your Odd page crops into your Even document in the correct reading order
  • Once complete, save document
  • Use the Printing Cropped Document as PDF instructions below to create an 8.5x11 resource document
  • Add title page as needed

Quality

Some quality issues you may encounter while scanning

While the type of book will impact the quality of the scan, there are several quality issues you will want to watch for while setting up your scanned pdf

Most common quality issues:

  • Gradient appearing on side or top
    • Usually caused by not enough pressure or uneven pressure being placed on the book while scanning. If appearing on top, can be caused by the top of the page being pressed against the frame of the scanner
  • Distorted text
    • Usually caused by the same issues as gradients
  • Unwanted Markings/smudges
    • Usually caused by something on the scanner which requires removing or cleaning
  • Slanted pages
    • Can be caused by uneven pressure or alignment while scanning, sometimes a side effect of scanning 2 pages at once (if continued issue, try scanning single pages)
  • Uneven/speckled page background
    • Sometimes unavoidable depending on the type of reading you are scanning. Try scanning in black and white if you are using greyscale, or adjusting the lightness during the scan
  • Note that depending on the original source, you may not be able to avoid all quality issues (for example some hardcovers make it impossible to scan a reading without some text distortion and gradient). The most important consideration is that all pages are consistent and as close to removing all quality issues as possible

Ideally a completed page after this point will look something like below (allowing some differences depending on the original book):

Printing Cropped Document as PDF

Once all the pages in your main working PDF meet the quality standards, you will need to print this document to a PDF.

Steps:

  • Under "File" select Print
  • Under the scrolldown menu next to "Printer:" select Adobe PDF
  • Under "Page Sizing and Handling" adjust settings to best fit document (with some blank margin space - most commonly the Shrink Oversized Page option works best unless the page is very large)
  • Under Properties you may want to adjust a few things to best fit the document (may require some testing)
    • Under Adobe PDF setting you may want to adjust the Default Setting to something nicer than Standard unless this makes the new PDF too large
    • Under Paper/Quality select whether you want it in color or not
  • Name the final document to regular course standards (ie COUR1234_authorlastname_booktitle)
  • Review final product - you may want to physically print one or two pages to make sure quality is correct

It may take several tries to get the correct setting

Extracting the Suggested Schedule

It is recommended to extract the Suggested Schedule as a separate document when formatting the Course Guide as it will need to be uploaded into Moodle as a Word document. Refer to Word/Print Formatting for further information.

Autolinking Moodle Resources (Files) and Activities

We use a Moodle function called autolinking which automatically links Moodle resources and activities to matching text (e.g. an assignment activity called “Assignment 1: Case Study (15%)” will automatically link anywhere “Assignment 1: Case Study (15%)” is used in the course container content).

Autolinking Activities (Assignmens, Quizzes, Discussions, etc.)

To autolink activities, we add the full activitiy name as a new paragraph with bold text, see example below. The autolinking text can be added directly to our Word documents to be scripted to XML.

Autolinking Resources (Uploaded Documents)

To autolink documents/resources that will be uploaded to the Moodle Resources or Assessments Overview sections. We can:

  • Confirm our resource files in Subversion are named correctly
  • In Word use the use the linking functionality (CTRL+K) to highlight the text we want to autolink and select the resource files
  • This will generate an Objectref tag in XML, which will help us indentify resources that need to be uploaded to Moodle and the correct Moodle resource titles.

Disabling Autolinked Text

In some instances we do not want text autolinked, for example main course headings H1-H5. In these instances, we can add the following tag in the Moodle text editor code view to disable the autolink:

<h2><span class="nolink">Assignment 1: Case Study (15%)</span></h2>

This will stop Moodle from automatically creating an "Assignment 1: Case Study (15%)" autolinked H2 heading.

Course Guide Assessment Table/Assessment Setup

  • The course assessment title/weight details will generally match the CG Assessment table information. If not please check with Production Supervisor.
  • If assessment title descrepacies can't be resolved in Production, we may need to contact that Course Lead for confirmation.
  • Once confirmed we need to notify csa@tru.ca of any assessment table changes (titles or weights)
  • The word "Mandatory" is not required to be included in the assessment table if it's included in the wording above the table (e.g To successfully complete this course, you must achieve a passing grade of 50% or higher on the overall course and 50% or higher on the mandatory Final Project.)
  • The Moodle Gradebook should match the same order as the Course Guide assessment table.

Additional Course Guide Wording

Some older courses/course guides may need to following wording added:

Assessments/Course Access After Completion

Add after the Course Guide/Assessments/Final Exam information:

Heading 3: Course Access After Completion
Paragraph: You will have access to your online course material and assessments in your learning management system for 60 days from the date of your final grade.

Help Available/Learning Strategist

Add after the Course Guide/Help Available/TRU Library information:

The Learning Strategists support student learning and well-being. They can help you navigate resources and support services, and they can answer general questions about Open Learning and the student engagement events on Out in the Open. They provide learning strategies, resources, and tips for students who may be struggling with different areas of online learning. Contact the Learning Strategist by phone, virtual appointment, or email at olconnect@tru.ca.

Addressing Production Notes

Production notes, distinguished by their blue font, are often included throughout the Word documents that are received. It is recommended to flag or address these, if possible, while formatting. Some may need to be addressed when editing in the XML environment. These may include, but are not limited to:

  • Instructions to include a note box
  • Instructions to create a discussion forum or assignment submission activity
  • Instructions to link to a particular file
  • Create or link to existing H5P content
  • Instructions to embed media – be sure to cross-reference with the Copyright Report
  • Instructions to create a show/hide activity
  • Request to fix an image

General Good Practice

As you are formatting Word documents, it is recommended that you flag any potential questions that you may have for the course lead, editor, or production supervisor. Flagging these items will also prove useful for the Production team member conducting an Internal Review, as it will provide additional context for any pending or completed changes that have been made causing differences between the content displayed in Moodle and the source documents.

Questions may relate to:

  • general formatting,
  • outdated terminology or Moodle instructions,
  • missing files or broken links,
  • unclear instructions,
  • inconsistencies between the module and topic titles between the Course Guide and Modules, or
  • general inconsistencies in formatting and/or instructions throughout the course.

You may also find it helpful to flag items for yourself that may require additional actions when editing in XML, such as adding block quotes.

item.title: Moodle Upgrade Checklist
item.dc:creator: hasslethishoff
item.content:encoded:
Adapted from A Practical Guide to Testing Moodle Mike Kelly (SonicCat Studios) for BCNET - September 24 2025: https://soniccat.notion.site/a-practical-guide-to-testing-moodle-20250924#277902a2e61d8062a174d32eca90f7bf

Open Learning Areas of Inspection

The following areas in Moodle should be reviewed after upgrading to ensure that no errors, layout issues, or data corruption have occurred. Test with standard permissions and as a student.

Prioritised / Practical Testing

  • Step 1: Begin with basic login tests across different user roles.
  • Step 2: Conduct initial checks on critical functionalities like course management and gradebook access. Expand to critical plugins.
  • Step 3: Engage users (teachers, students) to test specific features relevant to their roles.
  • Step 4: Review release notes to identify areas requiring deeper testing due to significant changes.
  • Step 5: Focus on known problematic areas from past upgrades.

Moodle Testing Checklist

1. User Interface and Navigation

  • Test Login: Verify login functionality for different user roles (admin, teacher, student).
  • Dashboard Check: Ensure the dashboard displays correctly and all links are functional.
  • Course Navigation: Navigate through courses to verify that pages load and render correctly.
  • Theme Consistency: Confirm that themes are applied consistently across all pages.
  • Browser Compatibility: Test in multiple browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge).
  • Mobile Compatibility: Confirm site functionality across multiple mobile devices and browsers (iPhones, iPads, Android phones and tablets, etc).
  • Mobile App: Confirm the Moodle mobile app has not been enabled due to upgrade

2. Course Management

  • Create a New Course: Verify the ability to create, edit, and delete courses.
  • Course Backup and Restore: Test course backup and restore functionality.
  • Enrolment Methods: Check that all enrolment methods work as expected (manual, self-enrol, database, etc).

3. Activities and Resources

  • Assignments: Test assignment creation, submission, grading, and feedback.
  • Quizzes: Verify quiz creation, settings (time limits, shuffle questions), attempts, and results.
  • Forums: Test forum creation, posting, replying, and moderation.
  • Wiki and Glossary: Check that wikis and glossaries can be created and edited.
  • URL Resources: Ensure external links open correctly within Moodle.
  • Uploads: Confirm that file uploads work as expected, including file-size upload limits.

4. Gradebook

  • Grade Calculation: Verify the accuracy of calculated grades.
  • Manual Grades: Test manual grade entry and updates.
  • Grade Export: Check that grades export properly to CSV or other formats.

5. Plugins and Extensions

  • Custom Plugins: Ensure any custom plugins are functional.
  • Third-Party Integrations: Verify tools like Turnitin, Kaltura, Zoom, etc.
  • Old Plugins: Make a list of older, unsupported plugins on your server and then try installing/using those plugins in a new course to see if they cause problems.

6. Security and Access Control

  • Role-Based Access: Verify and test permissions for different roles (admin, teacher, student).
  • Profile Privacy: Check that user profile settings are respected.
  • SSO/Authentication: If using SSO, ensure it works post-upgrade.

7. Performance Testing

  • Page Load Times: Monitor for slow-loading pages or timeouts.

8. Scheduled Tasks

  • Failing: Check for any scheduled tasks with a non-zero fail-delay.
  • Logs: Review individual failed task logs.

9. User Experience

  • Role-based testing: Log in as a user from each role (student, teacher/instructor/manager/admin) and verify the experience is as expected.

10. User Authentication Methods

  • Local Accounts: Test login with local accounts.
  • LDAP/SAML/SSO: Verify authentication via LDAP, SAML, etc., if used.

11. Communication Tools

  • Private Messaging: Ensure messaging between users works.
  • Notifications: Check that notifications are sent and received correctly.
  • Email: Verify that outgoing (and incoming, if applicable) email works

12. Documentation Review

  • User Guide: Update or verify existing documentation for the new version.
  • Changelog Review: Review Moodle's official version changelog for known issues (can be found on the Download page for each Moodle version).

13. Customizations

  • Theme Customizations: Ensure custom themes still work as expected.
  • Custom CSS: Test that any custom CSS still works properly
  • Custom Code: Test any custom PHP code or database changes.

14. Data Migration from older Moodle versions

  • Moodle Course Restore: Test restoring a Moodle course backup from an older version.
  • Data Integrity: Verify that all data (grades, activities) is correctly migrated.

15. Accessibility

  • Screen Reader Compatibility: Test with screen readers like JAWS or NVDA.
  • Keyboard Navigation: Ensure all functionality works without a mouse.

16. Third-Party Integrations

  • LTI Tools: Test integration with Learning Tools Interoperability (LTI) tools.
  • SIS Integration: Verify Student Information System (SIS) integrations.
  • Moodle’s WebAPI: Confirm Moodle WebAPI functionality (if you have apps and services which use it).

Container Examples

  • DEV_OL Content Samples - Standard Moodle Activities, Tabs, Interactive XML elements (show/hide, QA, etc.), audio/visual media
  • DEV_OL ENGL 1031_SW3 - Bootstrap Elements toggles and modals
  • DEV_OL VTEC 1211_ON1 - Videos and H5P (Modules/Books)
  • DEV_OL ANES 4071_SW2 - Tooltips
  • DEV_OL HIST 3741_SW1.1 - Image Gallery
  • DEV_OL STAT 1201_SW4 - WeBWorK

item.title: Final Step: Word to XML – Running QuickTagIt
item.dc:creator: hasslethishoff
item.content:encoded:
QuickTagIt is an XML scripting tool that is used to convert .docx files into .xml files at.O:\Open Learning Share\IDRG-production\SOFTWARE\QUICK TAG IT. It is recommended to create a shortcut on your desktop to the latest version.

The single .xml file should be saved in the root directory of the course in Subversion, or you may experience issues uploading images. It is recommended to convert each Word document to an XML file, then copy and paste whole objectgroups into a single file.

Name the file as follows: course code_version number.

  1. Start Quicktagit and select the Word document to be converted by using the browse button.
  2. The document must be a .docx file. If formatted properly the Course Acronym and Course Number will populate. You must enter a Course Title.
  3. Selecting “Convert All DOCX in Same Directory” will automatically convert any other .DOCX within the selected file and place it in the same XML document.
  4. The .xml output file is placed in the same spot as where the source document is located. You can leave word files within subversion Content folder.

item.title: XML Structure– Objectgroups and Topics
item.dc:creator: bforsyth
item.content:encoded:
Recent changes: Added Objectgroups and Course Structure section with standard tab layout order and updated Topic Suffix IDs with "_page" item

Objectgroups and topics are the basic organizational skeleton of any course XML. The most common course layout currently in use utilizes books. In this layout, the first objectgroup serves as the parent tab with the nested objectgroup serving as a book, and each topic acting as a page or chapter within the book.

Objectgroups

These are the basic building blocks of a course. Objectgroups may include things such as a “Course Guide”, tabs (like Assessments Overview, Modules, Discussions etc), or individual Modules (Module 1, Module 2 etc) if nested within the original Modules objectgroup. Topics are discussed below.

Objectgroups and Course Structure

Objectgroups will generally follow this order depending on the requirements for the course:

  • Course Guide (Welcome page)
  • Assessments Overview
  • Modules/Units/Lessons
  • Self-Tests
  • Discussions
  • Resources
  • Final Exam

Nested Objectgroups (Books and Subtabs)

In order to create books and subtabs you will need to nest objectgroups. These two forms are formatted near identically, but give different outputs.

Nesting Objectgroups for Books (Most Commonly Used Format)

For this format the first objectgroup will be the parent tab and the nested objectgroup will be the Book. Book pages or chapters are created using Topics.

For this format the first objectgroup will be the parent tab, and the nested objectgroup will be the subtab. Labels within the nested objectgroup will then appear as labels within the subtabs.

Overview of Attributes

  • id: Mandatory. make logical and readable. For example: CG or U1 or U1_overview or U1_topic1.
  • titletype: “titled” means it should have a <title> tag; “gentitle” means it will generate a title; “untitled”  means it will not have a title.

Topics

Topics exist within objectgroups. Topics are where the majority of the course content will exist (excluding resources and PDFs). You can add suffixes to a topic ID to make the topic appear as a forum (discussion), assignment activity, subchapter in a book, or resource placeholder.

Topics within a Book (most commonly used format)

Topics within a book will create a book chapter which will contain the basic content for that page.

Topic Suffix IDs

You can add a suffix to the topic id attribute in order to change a topic from a book chapter/ label to one of the following:

  • _page – page resource
  • _forum – forum activity
  • _assignment – assignment activity
  • _sub – sub chapter in a book
  • _resource – file resource placeholder

item.title: Formatting Content in XML for Moodle
item.dc:creator: bforsyth
item.content:encoded:
Headings 

Add a heading by selecting the “heading” element. To access the elements list, press enter and start to type the element name. You MUST add a heading level (1-5) to make it valid.

When converting a Word document to XML, level 1 headings are automatically converted to a new objectgroup (with the text as title). Heading level 2 in Word is automatically converted to a topic in XML. For this reason, we start at level 3 for the largest headings of the page, and go down to level 5 for the smallest.

You can also create a heading with an already set heading level through the following shortcuts:

Emphasis Text

The emphasis element covers a wide variety of text-altering options. The default <emphasis>text</emphasis> will result in italic text. To change it to something else you can change the “emphtype” attribute to one of the following:

  • Bold
  • Italic
  • Bold and Italic
  • Underline
  • Bold and Underline

Lists

To create a list, use the listcomplex element.

Nesting Lists (Multi-level Lists)

Multi-level lists can be created by nesting the listcomplex element within a listentry.

Tip: For complex lists, you may find it useful to briefly remove the visibility of tags in the Oxygen editing environment to have a better view of how lists are indented.

Adding External Links

External links can be added in one of two ways in an XML document:

  • Adding a direct URL link using the “url” element, or
  • Adding a hyperlink to text using the “weblink” element

URL Element

Weblink Element

Tables

Tables in XML are formatted similar to HTML. The “Table” element contains the table row (“tr”) element and the table cell (“td”) element.

TD Element

The “td” element is the main visible child element. No mandatory attributes need to be set; however, you may need to adjust the column span (colspan) or row span (rowspan) to match the source Word document.

This section covers the fillable textarea, and the print table function. For example, see HUMS 3531 SW1.

textarea

The textarea element in html places a box where students can enter as much text as they like. The text is not persistant! If the student leaves the page, their text is lost. They can save a copy by printing it. Normal page printing will not contain the text and requires special code available below.

By default the textarea is resizable (except on Internet Explorer), but this can be disabled with style="resize:none". Width and height are the cols and rows attribute. These attributes are not pixels! Instead they are by number of characters.

TextArea Attributes:

TextArea Styles:

Print Table

While the printable area code was meant for the textarea tables, you can use the code anywhere you would want to print only a small portion of a page. This print area cannot print iframes or other embedded interactive elements. For use with elements such as radio buttons, sliders, and checkboxes, use the extended code example below.

The printarea has these parts:

  • An encapsulating div container holding everything (Required)
  • A div with the class "printarea" that contains what you want to print
  • A hyperlink containing the print code outside the printarea but inside the first div container

The code relies on this structure, though if you wanted you could put the print hyperlink inside the printarea and it would then show up on the printed document. Use the code below as a template. You can edit the 'Print Table' text to whatever you like.

Code Example

<div>
<div class="printarea">

<!-- Your Content Here (Below is a textarea example) -->

<table><tbody><tr>
<td>
  <p>TextArea 1:</p>
  <textarea rows="7" cols="30" id="m01_a01_t01"></textarea>
</td><td>
  <p>TextArea 2:</p>
  <textarea rows="7" cols="30" id="m01_a01_t02" style="resize:none;"></textarea>
</td>
</tr></tbody></table>

<!-- End of Your Content -->

</div>
<p><a href="#" onclick="(function(e){
var area = $(this).closest('div').find('.printarea');
var areas = area.find('textarea').toArray();
for (i = 0; i < areas.length; ++i) {
areas[i].innerHTML = areas[i].value;
}
newDoc = window.open('');
newDoc.document.write(area.get(0).innerHTML);
newDoc.document.close();
newDoc.focus();
newDoc.print();
newDoc.close();
}).call(this); return false;">Print Table</a></p>
</div>

Extended Code Example

The following supports Radio Buttons and value based inputs such as sliders

<div>
<div class="printarea">

<!-- Your Content Here -->

</div>
<p><a href="#" onclick="(function(e){
var area = $(this).closest('div').find('.printarea');
var areas = [area.find('textarea').toArray(),area.find('input').toArray()];
for (i = 0; i < areas[0].length; ++i) {
areas[0][i].innerHTML = areas[0][i].value;}
for (i = 0; i < areas[1].length; ++i) {
areas[1][i].getAttribute('type') == 'radio' ? 
(areas[1][i].checked ? areas[1][i].setAttribute('checked','checked') :
areas[1][i].removeAttribute('checked')):
areas[1][i].setAttribute('value',areas[1][i].value);}
newDoc = window.open('');
newDoc.document.write(area.get(0).innerHTML);
newDoc.document.close();
newDoc.focus();
newDoc.print();
newDoc.close();
}).call(this); return false;">Print Activity</a></p>
</div>

Extended Inverse Code Example

The following puts the print link above the activities.

<div>
<p><a href="#" onclick="(function(e){
var area = $(this).closest('div').find('.printarea');
var areas = [area.find('textarea').toArray(),area.find('input').toArray()];
for (i = 0; i < areas[0].length; ++i) {
areas[0][i].innerHTML = areas[0][i].value;}
for (i = 0; i < areas[1].length; ++i) {
areas[1][i].getAttribute('type') == 'radio' ? 
(areas[1][i].checked ? areas[1][i].setAttribute('checked','checked') :
areas[1][i].removeAttribute('checked')):
areas[1][i].setAttribute('value',areas[1][i].value);}
newDoc = window.open('');
newDoc.document.write(area.get(0).innerHTML);
newDoc.document.close();
newDoc.focus();
newDoc.print();
newDoc.close();
}).call(this); return false;">Print Below Activity</a></p>
<div class="printarea">

<!-- Your Content Here -->

</div>
</div>

Note Boxes

Note boxes occur frequently within text and are usually requested through the use of a “production note” in the source Word document. Note boxes are often automatically generated when converting from Word, but may need to be created by selecting the “Note” element. A full range of elements can then be used within the note tag.

Attributes

Note box shading is controlled by the “role” attribute. A general title (NOTE:) can also be included by selecting “titletype” and then “gentitle.”

Example of note boxes in XML:

Example of note boxes rendering in Moodle:

Audio and Video Media

Overview

The “mediaobject” element allows us to embed a media player within our text, as well as any transcripts that need to go with the media.

This element is typically used to embed all Barabus (media server) links, as well as external links where possible, such as YouTube videos.

The “mediasource” element automatically generates within the “mediaobject” tags. The “mediasource” element contains the actual media link. This means that two sets of attributes need to be set:

Note: If the Barabus video appears to have black/blank thumbnail, please create a Media course subtask with all affected Barabus URLs and assign to Jon on the Media Team to update.

Inserting Videos from External Sources

Videos from external sources, such as YouTube, can also be embedded within the “mediaobject” element.

To do so, first find the embed code (if provided) on the external site, usually found by first selecting “Share.” The embed code will provide two key pieces of information:

  • The media link to be inserted in the “mediasource”tags.
  • The height and width to be set within the “mediasource” attributes

Transcript Element

The “transcript” element is another sub-element of the mediaobject tag and is placed AFTER the “mediasource” element. The transcript text must be formatted with standard “para” and list elements (see options given under elments). There are no specific attributes to set.

Video Submissions (Assignments and Activities) - Kaltura Instructions

If an assignment or activity is requesting students submit a video, the following needs to be included. Adjust the wording for non-assignment or ungraded activities if needed.

  1. Clear instructions on length
  2. A notebox with the following information code snippet:
<div class="noteInsetbox"><h5 class="noteTitle">Video Submission</h5><p>Please <b>DO NOT</b> upload video files directly to the assessment submission activity. Use the Embed Kaltura Media button in the text editor to upload/capture your video after selecting the Add Submission button below.</p>
    <p><img src="IMAGEURLHERE" alt="An image highlighting the location of the Kaltura Embed Media button in the Moodle text editor." width="820" height="100" class="img-fluid"><br></p>
<p>Refer to the Open Learning Student Guide for additional information on how to add a video to your assessment submission.</p>
</div>

Linking Files: Inserting Images, Figures, & Equations

File Naming

It is common that received files are not named appropriately and need to be renamed in the following format:

  • Start with course code
  • Briefly indicate the location of the file within the course content
  • For works with an author, put the first author name next
  • For images, indicate the figure number, caption, or a brief identifiable description
  • Replace spaces with “_” or remove
  • Avoid special characters
  • Examples:
    • MNGT4781_M1_T5_Stillman.pdf
    • MNGT4781_M1_T1_Fig3.png

File Renaming

  • For just a few files, individual renaming works fine (F2 is short cut to open rename feature)
  • If you have many files with similiar renaming issues (ie. removing all spaces and replacing with “_”), then an automated tool helps.

The following web site details a few methods you can use in Windows to rename multiple files: http://www.howtogeek.com/111859/how-to-batch-rename-files-in-windows-4-ways-to-rename-multiple-files/.

  1. Open Power Shell (find under Accessories, choose Power Shell version to open command window)
  2. You will need to be in the same directory where your files are so change the directory as needed.
  3. change directory command: cd <pathname>  where <pathname> is the location where you want to run command. If your pathname has spaces it will need to be in quotes.

Example:

Powershell opens with command prompt:

PS H:\>

Files are located in: C:\Users\cteare\Desktop\ANES4005\Content\PowerPoint Presentations

First step is to change directory by entering the following at command prompt

cd “C:\Users\cteare\Desktop\ANES4005\Content\PowerPoint Presentations”

NOTE:

  • Do not type all of the above in
  • Type “cd” then grab the pathname from Windows explorer by right-clicking in bar and selecting “copy.”
  • Right click beside “cd” and it will paste in
  • Move cursor to where need to go and type them in
  • Hit “Enter” and prompt should change to PS <new pathname>:
  • Run command to switch spaces to _
  • dir | rename-item -NewName {$_.name -replace ” “,”_”}
  • Type: Exit to close shell window

Adding Graphic Entities

Prior to adding any type of file (PDF, Word, Excel, image etc.) to XML, they must be first listed as a graphic entity. Graphic entities can be added at any time and do not have to all be added at once. Ensure that you have followed the Associated File Prep steps above to ensure your files have been named correctly and placed in the appropriate file locations.

To add graphic entities in Oxygen, follow these steps:

  1. Ensure that you have installed the Graphic Entity tool, found in O:\Open Learning Share\IDRG-production\DEVELOPMENT\_OXYGEN_XML\GraphicEntityButton.
    You may need to restart Oxygen Editor and make screen adjustments until you can see the “Graphic Entity” button.
  2. Select the “Graphic Entity” button.
  3. You will be prompted to select one or more files to add as entities, and then select “Make Entity References.”
  4. If successful, you will receive a notification that all files have been added as entities.

Linking Files Using the Objectref Element

The “objectref” element is used to link to a file after it has been added as an entity using the method detailed above. To do so:

  1. Insert the “objectref” element.
  2. Fill in required Attributes.
    • entity: select the file you wish to link to
    • pointsTo: select the type of entity you are pointing to, usually “file.”
    • title: usually the same text that is contained within the “objectref” tags.

IMPORTANT:
We use a Moodle function called autolinking which automatically links Moodle resources and activities to matching text (e.g. an uploaded file called "Module 1 PowerPoint" will automatically link anywhere "Module 1 PowerPoint" is used in the course container).
In almost all cases, objectref tags indicate files that will need to be uploaded to a Resources section/tab in the Moodle course and should automatically link within the course content.

Inserting Images Using the Image Element

The “image” element is used to insert an image after it has been added as an entity using the method detailed above. To do so:

  1. Add the “image” element (will be automatically nested within the 'figure' element).
  2. Fill in the required Attributes:
    • alt: the text that will be displayed if the image does not load correctly.
    •  entity: select the image that you wish to insert
    • height/ width: should generate automatically, but can adjust if you wish to make the image smaller or larger.

Note: Images will automatically be center-aligned when displayed in Moodle

Adding Captions and Attributions

There are two elements generally used when adding captions, credit lines, or figure titles to an image: the “caption” element and the “attribution” element.

  • The caption element creates a line of normal size text which will appear bold and exactly centered in-line with the image. Used for titles and captions, but is sometimes used for other things such as credit lines (indicated in 'Material Caption' column in Copyright Report).
  • The attribution element creates a line of smaller than standard text. Most commonly this is used for credit lines, but is sometimes requested for other uses.
    Attributions will normally be indicated in the “Material Credit Line Text” column of the Copyright Report.

See below for an example:

Interactive Elements

QA Element

The “QA” element is used to create simple Question/Answer scenarios, such as:

  • Show/Hide content
  • Simple Multiple Choice
  • True/False
  • Short Answer
  • Matching

When the “QA” element is created, the question tags will automatically generate. Next, place the cursor just to the left of the closing “qa” tag and press enter to create one of the following elements:

  • “answer” – results in a simple show/hide answer.
  • “option” – used to create an answer that can be set as a “distractor” or a “key”

Multiple Choice

  • Add the QA tag, change type attribute to multiple-choice, add a PARA tag, and the question. (Note: If you want the questions numbered, add the number before your question, as numbers aren't automatically added.)
  • Add one OPTION tag for each possible answer.
  • Change the type attribute of the correct answer to 'key'. All others should be 'distractor'.
  • Add an ANSWER tag with "Correct" text or other feedback that students will see when they select the right answer

True/ False

  • Add the QA tag, change type attribute to multiple-choice, add a PARA tag, and the question.
  • Add a OPTION tag with "True" and other OPTION tag with "False".
  • Change the type attribute of the correct answer to 'key' and keep the incorrect answer as 'distractor'.
  • Add an ANSWER tag with "Correct" text or other feedback that students will see when they select the right answer

Short Answer

  • Add the QA tag, change type attribute to short-answer, add a PARA tag, and the question.
  • Add as many ANSWER tags needed to capture variations in student response (e.g. 2, Two and two in the example provided).
  • For each ANSWER tag, set the checktype to exact.

Matching (Using Short Answer)

  • Create a table with two columns and one row per question needed and add column titles as needed (e.g. Description and Name in the example)
  • In the right-hand column, select the second set of TD tags and adjust the rowspan attribute to match the number of rows/question (e..g. 3 in the example)
  • In the same column, add your matching items starting with "A. MatchingText", "B. MatchingText" "C. MatchingText", etc. as students will input the letter as the answer.
  • Add the QA tag in the left-hand column/row, change type attribute to short-answer, add a PARA tag, and the question.
  • Add as many ANSWER tags needed to capture variations in student response (e.g. b, B, b., B. in the example provided).
  • For each ANSWER tag, set the checktype to exact.
  • Repeat steps 4 through 6 for each matching question as needed.

Tooltips (Text Pop-up On Click)

Tooltips allow students to click on linked text to show more information in a pop-up box. Often used as a glossary.

Tooltip example: DEV_OL ANES 4071_SW2 - Research Skills for Anesthesia Assistants

  1. Use the tooltiplink tag to create the linked text, add reference in Attribute (e.g. m1_1)
  2. Use to tooltip tag to display text/content when linked text is clicked, add id in Attribute panel. Note that the reference and id Attributes must match for tooltip to work

Tooltiplink Tag and Reference

Tooltip Tag and Id

Inserting Font Awesome Icons

Note: Our version of Moodle uses Font Awesome 4. Use the link provided below to see available icons.

Icon Formatting

Icons can be added directly into the XML or HTML code using shortcodes from the Font Awesome Icon Library.
For example, [fa-users] included the in XML or HMTL will appear as the following icon in Moodle:

Sizing

You can also add sizing to the Font Awesome shortcode in the XML or HTML by adding fa-3x (or any that appear here) to the shortcode, for example, [fa-users fa-3x], and appear as:

Placing Font Awesome shortcodes within a H2 tag will give you the same sizing and colouring as the H2 text.

item.title: Content Review
item.dc:creator: bforsyth
item.content:encoded:
Once you have converted a Word file to XML, you will need to compare the XML to the source document. You will remove or add formatting as necessary, and ensure accuracy to the source material.

Highlight text in the Word document that is likely to be problematic such as italicized/underlined/bold text, superscripts, and subscripts for easy review. Here are a number of common conversion errors to watch out for and manual edits that are required in the XML environment:

Course Guide

  • In the Course Guide, ensure the Course Description, Course Requisites (prerequisites and Exclusions), and Learning Outcomes have been placed in an “Approved” notebox.

Headings

  • Ensure that heading levels have accurately converted.

Hanging Indents

  • Hanging indents must be added to <para> tags of Resources (readings and videos) and References sections.

Symbols

  • Watch for complicated symbols that may not convert, such as checkmarks found in Activity Checklists.

Lists

  • Multiple list levels may not always accurately convert, i.e. may not be correctly nested or may display the incorrect list type (bullet, number, letter). Refer to Lists under Formatting Content.
  • Paragraph tags will often be missing in lists with multiple (nested) list levels. Add <para> tag to ensure correct spacing.

Quotes

  • Use blockquote tag to centre align quotes that appear as a separate paragraph within the course content. Text must be included within a paragraph tag to work correctly.

Example of how the blockquote appears in Moodle:

Superscripts/Subscripts

  • Watch for superscripts and subscripts that do not convert. These can be added in the XML by highlighting the relevant text and adding the “sub” or “super” element as needed.

Once you have completed your review of the XML, you are ready to import the course content into Moodle. Refer to Importing Course Content into Moodle (XML to HTML) for further information.

item.title: Moodle Assignment Setup & Settings
item.dc:creator: hasslethishoff
item.content:encoded:
Assignment Settings

  • See Moodle Rubrics for how to set up a rubric

Keep default settings for Tags.

Alternate (ALT) Assignments

If we are given two sets of assignment files (ALT or alternate assignments) they will be scripted to XML and uploaded to Moodle as pages (_page in XML) and hidden using Group access restrictions with additional instructions for the OLFM.

View DEV_OL MATH 1071_SW4 - Fundamentals of Mathematics for Business and Economics as an example of alternate assignments.

In XML Assessments Overview section:

  • Include the ALT assignment instruction and include _page in the topic title to generate a Page resource in Moodle
  • Include a topic tag at the bottom of the section with the following OLFM instructions:

H2: Alternate Assignment Setup for Open Learning Faculty Members

This course includes alternate (ALT) assignment instruction for instances where another submission is required, but new assignment material is required. The ALT assignments are included in the same section as the main assessments and are currently hidden from student view. Use the Participants/Groups settings to allow access to specific students.

  • Navigate to the Participants section, click the dropdown menu and select Groups
  • Select the Group/ALT assignment you want to make visible for the student(s) and click the Add/remove users button
  • Select the student(s) details in the right-hand column and click the Add button.
  • All students in a group will have access to that corresponding ALT assignment

Once a student has been added to a Group, you can direct the student to the ALT assignment instructions and allow another submission on the corresponding assignment activity.

If you require additional support regarding adding a student to groups in Moodle, please refer to the OLFM HUB resource in Moodle or contact Moodle Support if additional assistance is required.

In Moodle:

  • Hide the Alternate Assignment Setup for Open Learning Faculty Members information we added above.
  • Move each ALT assignment Page underneath the corresponding Assignment Activity
  • Navigate to the Participants section, and select Groups.
  • Create a corresponding group for each alternate assignment we have in Moodle. (e.g. Assignment 1 - ALT, Assignment 2 - ALT, etc.)
  • For each ALT Assignment Page or related Resource file
    • Go to the Edit Settings section and scroll down to the Restrict access options
    • Click the Add restriction button (1) and select the Group option
    • Click the eye icon (2) and choose the corresponding ALT assignment Group (3)
    • Confirm Restricted message below ALT assignment is visible and correct. E.g. Restricted - Not available unless: You belong to Assignment 1 - ALT (hidden otherwise)

Note: With the new ALT setup, assignments should not be hidden from students using the Edit dropdown in the Assignments/Assessments Overview section. We should see the Restricted message as noted above.

Assignment Related Resources (Files)

If the assignment requires additional resources or instructions that are provided in files (e.g. PDF, Word, etc.) we need to:

  • Tag the file resource with the objectref tag in XML
  • Upload the files to the Assignment/Assessment Overview tab and insert/indent the resource underneath the corresponding assignment activity
  • Ensure the resource is autolinked within the assignment activity

Assignments with Video Submissions

If a course is requesting a video submission, we need the following:

  1. Clear instructions on length
  2. A notebox with following information:

IMPORTANT:
Please DO NOT attach videos directly in the assignment submission point. Use the Embed Kaltura Media button in the text editor as shown here: Kaltura Video Upload Instructions

  1. To upload the Kaltura Video Upload Instructions PDF in the Assignment/Assessments Overview section and autolinked in the assignment activity
  2. To update the assignment activity settings to allow online text submissions

Assignments Using the Quiz Activity

In some instances where randomization is requires for assignments, we'll use the Moodle Quiz activity to present the assignment material. If that is the case, there are some additional instructions that need to be added to the XML and Moodle container to avoid student confusion.

is a good example that highlights the additional instructions added to the Assignments/Assessments Overview and Quiz activities.

  • DEV_OL SOCW 2121_SW4.1 - Social Welfare in Canada
  • DEV_OL COMP 1131_SW3.1 - Computer Programming I (File submission required)
  • DEV_OL COMP 1231_SW3.1 - Computer Programming II (File submission required)

Please add the following instructions and adjust as needed based on setup/requirements.

Assignments/Assessments Overview Instructions

Insert a caution (yellow) notebox below the full name/student ID number information:

IMPORTANT: Assignment and Quiz Activity Information
Many of your course assignments are completed using the Moodle Quiz activity. These Quiz activities can be found below and also by selecting the Quizzes link in Activities Block. Review the Overview and Instructions sections when necessary, and confirm any time limits for the assessment activities before you start. If you have accommodations that provide for extra time limits, please contact your Open Learning Faculty Member to arrange.

To save a section of your assignment using the Quiz activity, you must press the Next page button, and once your assignment is complete, press the Finish attempt button.

Assignment/Quiz Activity Instructions

If applicable, add the following wording below the assignment instructions:

There is no time limit for completion of this assignment. Once you select "Attempt Quiz Now" you will have access to assessment until you select "Submit all and Finish" button. You can leave and return to the assignment/quiz activity once you start.

Also, add the following notebox:

Note:
Your work saves automatically as you move from page to page in this activity.  You can edit any answer up to the point you submit the whole assignment. To force a save while working on a longer question, move from the activity page you are on to another one and back. The # sign icon in the editor will tell you have many words you have written. All text boxes expand as you type. 

Final Steps

Each assignment/quiz activity should include a description on the final page of the quiz with the following wording:
Once you have uploaded your assignment file and wish to submit. Please click "Finish attempt" then "Submit all and finish" buttons.

Assignment/Quiz Activity Structure

  • In the first question/description in an H3 full assignment title (e.g. "Assignment 1: Data and Expressions (4%)" and an H4 "Instructions" heading.
  • If the essay question type is required, but students submit a file at the end of the assignment add "(Ignore the text box below, your submission can be uploaded to the final question)" below each question.
  • In the quiz navigation, divide the quiz into the main sections where applicable:
    • Assignment instructions and questions - Full assignment title in quiz sidebar
    • Assignment Submission - If students are submitting files at the end, similar to standard assignment
    • Final Steps - Include a description with the wording noted above
